45 When referring to the applicant’s affidavit, her Honour stated there was no indication
that the applicant admitted guilt for these offences or had remorse or insights into the
impacts of his offending. Furthermore, there was no acknowledgement that his drug
problems were connected to the offences. Her Honour said other evidence suggested
in the opinions of certain people that the applicant had shown remorse. Her Honour
then said whilst it may be the case the applicant was remorseful for having sexual
contact with a girl he barely knew in circumstances where his “partner that night” was in
an adjoining granny flat, she was unable “to make a positive finding that he is in fact
remorseful for committing sexual offences against [MG] without her consent”.
46 The judge found, notwithstanding that finding, that the offences were an aberration, out
of character and “occurred in circumstances where, because of his use of cocaine that
evening that affected his judgment”.
47 Other findings that the judge made were that the applicant was unlikely to re-offend and
had reasonable prospects of rehabilitation.
48 The judge noted that the applicant’s parents lived in Victoria and suffered various
degrees of ill health. Her Honour accepted that would make the applicant’s time in
custody harder for him.
49 The judge stated that general deterrence was an important consideration in sentencing
for the present type of offences. When referring to specific deterrence, her Honour did
not consider there was any real or particular need for specific deterrence, other than
could be addressed by the imposition of the sentence.
50 Her Honour announced her intention to impose an aggregate sentence and considered
issues of accumulation, concurrence and totality for the sentence. Whilst accepting that
the applicant’s offending could have stopped at count 1, her Honour found that the
three offences were in fact one criminal episode and only slight accumulation was
warranted.
51 Her Honour found special circumstances, being the applicant’s age, his first time in
custody, the distance from his family, the health of his parents and that he remains drug
free upon release.
52 After indicating the sentences that would have been imposed, the judge imposed the
aggregate sentence: see [2]-[3] above.
Ground 1: Her Honour erred in her assessment of the objective criminality with respect
to Count 1 and elevated the indicative sentence which informs the aggregate sentence
53 The applicant referred to the circumstance of aggravation for count 1 being “knowing

Ground 1: Her Honour erred in her assessment of the objective criminality with respect
to Count 1 and elevated the indicative sentence which informs the aggregate sentence
53 The applicant referred to the circumstance of aggravation for count 1 being “knowing
that persons were inside the home” and that the particular act of sexual intercourse was
fellatio which lasted only “a couple of seconds”. The applicant pointed out that there
was an absence of force, violence, threat or intimidation.
54 The applicant submitted that the offence lay well below the mid-range given the various
assessments of the component parts of the offence.
55 In oral submissions, Ms Kluss, the applicant’s counsel, argued that the objective
criminality of the offence “making up count 1 was low range and even considering the
nature of the sexual assault [was] … less than mid-range ... given the variety of
circumstances with which a sexual assault can be considered.”
56 The Crown submitted that the absence of aggravating features is not a matter of
mitigation. Furthermore, there was no hierarchy of seriousness of different types of acts
of sexual intercourse which inform a finding of objective seriousness. The Crown
argued that it is the whole of the circumstances in which the offence was committed
that inform the assessment of objective seriousness.
57 Ms Kluss accepted that the lack of more serious objective factors did not amount to
mitigation but pointed to the fact that what might normally be anticipated in such
offending was not present and was relevant to the assessment of the objective
seriousness of the offence.
Consideration
58 The assessment of the objective seriousness of an offence “is quintessentially for the
sentencing judge”. [1] This Court has been “very slow” to determine such matters for
itself or to set aside such an assessment made by a sentencing judge. [2] As Hoeben
CJ at CL observed in Field v R [2020] NSWCCA 105 at [51]:
“The difficulties in intervening in such a determination are at their height in
circumstances where there has been a trial in which the sentencing judge has been
able to assess the evidence of the witnesses.”
59 The judge characterised the offence as falling “around or perhaps just under the middle
range for an offence of its type considered objectively”. The question is whether that
finding was open on the evidence.
60 The terms of count 1 of which the applicant had been found guilty were that the

range for an offence of its type considered objectively”. The question is whether that
finding was open on the evidence.
60 The terms of count 1 of which the applicant had been found guilty were that the
applicant “did break and enter the dwelling house of [MG]” and then in the house “did
commit a serious indictable offence, namely sexual intercourse without consent, in
circumstances of aggravation, namely, knowing that there was a person or persons
present in the said dwelling house”.
61 It is trite to observe that there is no gradation of the six circumstances of aggravation
defined in s 105A of the Crimes Act. [3] Furthermore, there is no hierarchy of sexual acts
that constitute sexual intercourse. [4]
62 When sentencing for an offence under s 112(2) of the Crimes Act, this Court has stated
on previous occasions that the assessment of the objective gravity of the offence is to
be made by reference to all the facts and circumstances of the case. [5] The focus of the
sentencing judge is to be on what the offender actually did and not on some
hypothetical scale of objective seriousness of either the circumstances of aggravation
or the act of sexual intercourse.
63 What then did the applicant do in committing the offence?
64 In the early hours of the morning, the applicant opened MG’s room having broken into
the house by climbing onto the roof and entering through a closed but unlocked
window. The judge accepted that the applicant had an interest to get back into the
home to retrieve his mobile phone and was unable to be satisfied that he planned to
sexually assault MG when he broke and entered the house. However, he decided to
engage in sexual activity with MG after entering her bedroom, then removing his
clothes and forcing his penis into her mouth whilst she was asleep in her bed. He told
MG to “suck it” after she woke and his penis remained in her mouth.
65 As the judge found, the applicant was in effect a stranger to MG who had not engaged
in any behaviour that could have led him to believe that any sexual activity would be
consensual. Furthermore, MG was asleep at the time when she was sexually assaulted
in this way. The applicant also had some idea that MG was either intoxicated and/or
tired when Ms M found her asleep on the toilet and took her upstairs.
66 Although the offence was of short duration, the introduction of the applicant’s penis into

tired when Ms M found her asleep on the toilet and took her upstairs.
66 Although the offence was of short duration, the introduction of the applicant’s penis into
the mouth of a sleeping woman was a serious sexual assault. As her Honour said, this
was a “particularly intimate act of fellatio”. The absence of force, violence or threat of
intimidation did not mitigate the objective seriousness of the offence, as MG was asleep
at the time.
67 In my view, it was open to the judge to find that the objective seriousness of the offence
was “around or perhaps just under” the middle of the range and no error has been
demonstrated.
68 I would dismiss this ground of appeal.
Ground 2: Her Honour imposed a sentence that was unreasonable or plainly unjust (for
reasons that may not be able to discern) and the sentence is manifestly excessive
69 The applicant further submitted that if the judge’s assessment of the objective gravity of
count 1 was accepted the resultant sentence remained manifestly excessive. The
applicant acknowledged that sentencing statistics were not provided to the judge,
however, provided sentencing statistics for an offence contrary to s 112(2) of the
Crimes Act to this Court. The applicant contended that even with an adjustment for an
assumed maximum utilitarian discount, the statistics demonstrated that the applicant’s
sentence sits at the top of the range despite her Honour’s objective assessment of the
offending.
70 Ms Kluss told this Court in oral submissions that no issue was taken with the marginal
accumulation attributed by the judge to the third and fourth counts. The applicant’s
focus, Ms Kluss said, was on count 1 which rendered the aggregate sentence
manifestly excessive.
71 The applicant contended that the unusual circumstances of the offences and the
applicant’s strong subjective case “boded for a lower indicative sentence and
consequently a lower aggregate sentence”.
72 The Crown submitted that the applicant’s focus on statistics for count 1 was
misconceived as an aggregate sentence was imposed. The Crown argued that the
indicative sentences announced by the judge in respect of each count were not
themselves excessive. Furthermore, the judge paid proper regard to the importance of
general deterrence and to the applicant’s subjective case. The Crown pointed out that
the judge’s findings concerning totality had not been challenged and there was a large
degree of concurrency in the aggregate sentence.
73 Another matter that the Crown raised was the significant reduction in the statutory ratio

the judge’s findings concerning totality had not been challenged and there was a large
degree of concurrency in the aggregate sentence.
73 Another matter that the Crown raised was the significant reduction in the statutory ratio
as the overall non-parole period was 59% of the overall term of the aggregate
sentence.
Consideration
74 This Court has often stated that to succeed on a ground where a complaint of manifest
excess is made, the applicant must establish that the sentence was unreasonable or
plainly unjust. [6] Consideration of whether a sentence is unreasonable or plainly unjust
is undertaken in the context that there is no single correct sentence and that sentencing
is not a mathematical exercise. Sentencing judges are required to reach a sentence for
an offence by balancing many different and conflicting features. [7] It follows that
sentencing judges are to be allowed as much flexibility as is consonant with
consistency of approach and applicable sentencing principles. [8]
75 The applicant’s argument of manifest excess is founded upon the submission that the
judge’s indicative sentence for count 1 was manifestly excessive which resulted in the
aggregate sentence being manifestly excessive.
76 The applicant does not challenge the judge’s assessment of the objective seriousness
of counts 3 and 4 or her Honour’s findings on his subjective case.
77 The challenge to the indicative sentence for count 1 was mainly based on JIRS
sentencing statistics for offences under s 112(2) of the Crimes Act. The limitations on
the utility of statistics are well known, but are more so in offences under s 112(2) as the
offence can be committed in a variety of ways. The lack of identification of the type of
serious indictable offence committed during the break and enter exacerbates this issue.
Another difficulty is that the statistics do not record the aggravating feature of an
offender being on conditional liberty at the time of the offending, as was the case with
the applicant.
78 Further, the applicant did not refer to any specific cases contained within the statistics.
Bearing in mind these substantial limitations, I note that with respect to the statistics for
not guilty pleas (of which there were only two), one received the same sentence as the
applicant’s indicative sentence and non-parole period for the s 112(2) offence, while the
other received a lesser sentence. As to the guilty pleas where a custodial sentence was
imposed, even when adjusted for a 25% utilitarian discount, the indicative sentence sits
within the middle of the range.

other received a lesser sentence. As to the guilty pleas where a custodial sentence was
imposed, even when adjusted for a 25% utilitarian discount, the indicative sentence sits
within the middle of the range.
79 Count 1 is a serious offence. The maximum penalty for this offence is 20 years
imprisonment with a standard non-parole period of 5 years. The judge did not err in her
assessment of the objective seriousness of the offence and gave careful consideration
to the applicant’s subjective circumstances.
80 I am not persuaded that the indicative sentence for count 1 is manifestly excessive.
81 In any event, the assessment of an indicative sentence as being excessive does not
mean that the aggregate sentence is excessive. [9] As was said by R A Hulme J in JM at
[40]:
“[the] principal focus of determination of a ground alleging manifest … excess will be
whether the aggregate sentence reflects the totality of the criminality involved.”
82 In my opinion, the aggregate head sentence appropriately reflects the totality of the
applicant’s offending and his subjective case. There was a modest accumulation of the
sentences for counts 3 and 4 and a finding of special circumstances which resulted in a
non-parole period of 59%.
83 The ultimate constraint on a finding of special circumstances is that the aggregate non-
parole period must appropriately reflect the criminality involved in the offences. [10] I am
of the view that the non-parole period of three years and three months is the minimum
period that the applicant should spend in custody.
84 I have concluded that the aggregate sentence is not manifestly excessive. I would
dismiss this ground of appeal.
Orders
85 I propose the following orders:
(1) Leave to appeal granted.
(2) Appeal dismissed.
86 N ADAMS J: I have had the advantage of reading in draft the judgment of Price J. I
agree with the orders proposed for the reasons provided by his Honour. Count 1 was
committed in the context that the applicant had gone home with the victim’s flatmate
and found the victim asleep on the toilet whilst intoxicated. The victim had to be taken
to bed by her flatmate. Hours later, whilst the victim was asleep in her bed in her own
house, the applicant climbed onto her roof, entered her bedroom through her closed but
unlocked bedroom window and she awoke to find his penis in her mouth. The fact that

house, the applicant climbed onto her roof, entered her bedroom through her closed but
unlocked bedroom window and she awoke to find his penis in her mouth. The fact that
he did not enter the premises to sexually assault her does not mean that this was not a
serious example of an offence contrary to s 112(2) of the Crimes Act 1900 (NSW). No

1 As the name suggests, Toorak Winery Pty Ltd ("the Winery") has for many
years operated a business producing, packaging and selling wine out of
winery premises located in Toorak Road, Leeton. On 13 March 2008, Mr
Raymond Gooley was working for the company as a Cellar Hand having
previously worked for the company during the 2004 vintage and being
employed as a casual Cellar Hand from October 2007. Mr Gooley's duties
included operating plant, including the press, potter bin and potters as well
as general cellar work.
2 On 13 March 2008, Mr Gooley was assigned to work known as "pressing
potters" on bin P4, a process that involved draining the juice from the potter

as general cellar work.
2 On 13 March 2008, Mr Gooley was assigned to work known as "pressing
potters" on bin P4, a process that involved draining the juice from the potter
tank via a press and transferring the juice into a wine storage tank. The
initial draining from the potter was first carried out using a draining hose
and when the flow of juice stopped, the hose would be manually drained out
and the potter bin rolled below the tank to be emptied. During the course of
this process, Mr Gooley opened the bottom door of the potter and an
apparent blockage suddenly cleared and a substantial amount of liquid and
skins rapidly escaped, hitting the sides of the potter bin. The force of the
expelled contents caused the potter bin to move, trapping Mr Gooley
between the edge of the potter bin and a stationary platform. Mr Gooley
received severe crush injuries and later died.
3 Following an investigation, Inspector Yates commenced prosecution
proceedings against the company alleging a breach of s 8(1) of the
Occupational Health and Safety Act 2000. The Application for Order alleged
a failure by the company to ensure the health, safety and welfare at work of
all its employees and in particular Mr Raymond Gooley. In an Amended
Application for Order, the following particulars were supplied:
The particulars of the risk are that:
(a) The health and safety of the employees of the defendant was
put at risk as they were exposed to the risk of injury from being
hit, trapped or crushed by moving plant, namely the potter bin
(including the potter bin platform).
The particulars of the acts or omissions in failing to eliminate the
risk are that:
(b) The defendant failed to provide and ensure that plant
provided for use by employees at work at the premises, namely,
the potter bin (including the potter bin platform) was safe and
without risk to health, and, in particular:
(i) the defendant failed to ensure that the movement of
the potter bin when not powered was controlled or
restricted, such as by the use of moveable wheel chocks,
wheel brakes or by anchoring the potter bin so as to
prevent the potter bin from inadvertent movement.
(c) The defendant failed to provide and ensure that plant
provided for use by employees at work at the premises, namely,
the potter bin (including the potter platform) and the adjacent
vinomatic platform was safe and without risk to health in that
the defendant failed to undertake measures as follows:

provided for use by employees at work at the premises, namely,
the potter bin (including the potter platform) and the adjacent
vinomatic platform was safe and without risk to health in that
the defendant failed to undertake measures as follows:
(i) ensuring that the potter bin was restricted from
unintended or expected movement underneath the

move under the vinomatic platform such as by the use of

not move or interact with the vinomatic platform to
create a pinch point between the edge of the potter bin
and the edge of the vinomatic platform; or

platform when it moved underneath the vinomatic
platform.
(d) The defendant failed to provide and maintain a safe system
of work for the task of pressing potters at the premises in that it
failed to undertake measures as follows:
(i) ensuring that the pinch points created by the
movement of the potter bin (including the potter bin
platform) were identified to employees.
(e) The defendant failed to conduct an adequate risk assessment
in relation to the task of pressing potters and in particular:
(i) the defendant failed to identify adequately the risk of
injury arising from the pinch points and determine how
the risk could be eliminated or controlled.
(f) The defendant failed to provide its employees with adequate
information, instruction and training in relation to the use and

(i) ensuring that employees were provided with training

of working with the plant and in particular of pinch points;
(ii) ensuring that employees were provided with

(iii) ensuring that employees were informed that the

and cause a possible crushing injury to an employee on
the potter bin platform.
As a result of the defendant's failure and omissions, employees were
placed at risk of injury and in particular, Raymond Gooley, did suffer

4 On the third listing of the matter and following case conferencing, the
defendant company entered a plea of guilty. At the hearing to receive
evidence and submissions on sentence, the prosecutor relied upon the
following documents:
(a) an Agreed Statement of Facts;
(b) two factual inspection reports prepared by Inspector Yates;
(c) two sets of photographs taken by Inspectors;
(d) two prohibition notices issued to the defendant by Inspector Yates on
13 and 18 March 20008; and
(e) an ASIC company search for Toorak Winery Pty Ltd.
The Agreed Statement of Facts acknowledged that the defendant
company had no prior relevant criminal convictions in New South Wales
and also contained a description of the work process in which Mr Gooley
was involved on the day of the accident. The Agreed Statement of Facts
appears as an annexure to this judgment.
5 The defendant company, in its case, read two affidavits: one affidavit
sworn by Mr Vincent Bruno, a director and secretary of the defendant
company, and, another affidavit sworn by Mr Robert Bruno, a wine maker
employed by the defendant company.
6 Mr Vincent Bruno spoke of the Winery being incorporated in 1988 and that
he had commenced as a director in 1989. His brother was also a director of
the Winery. The Bruno family had made wine at the premises since 1965.
He had also worked at the Winery since that date. Mr Vincent Bruno had
responsibility for overseeing the Winery in relation to production and sales
and that had been his role since 1965. His brother was responsible for
overseeing the operation of the vineyard. The two brothers had been
responsible, as owners, for the financial decisions made concerning the
viability of the operation in a volatile industry. He spoke of the task that
they had both undertaken and that, "during vintage", everybody assisted
and would help in the cellar. It was not unusual at this time to work up to
sixteen hours a day, seven days a week.
7 The usual Winery staff comprised of six "core" members who were
employed on a permanent basis and performed work on the farm, in the
cellar, the laboratory and the office. The biggest period of the year was

7 The usual Winery staff comprised of six "core" members who were
employed on a permanent basis and performed work on the farm, in the
cellar, the laboratory and the office. The biggest period of the year was
"vintage" and that was when the grapes were picked and the wine was
made. Vintage usually ran for approximately eight weeks from early
February to early April and during this period, the Winery was open for extra
days and extended hours. During vintage, casual labour was engaged to
assist with the added workload and for the 2008 vintage, four casual
employees were engaged. Mr Gooley was one of the casuals so employed.
8 Mr Vincent Bruno spoke of the potter fermentation system that had been
in operation at the Winery for over 30 years. This system was used for

He had seen this operation in a number of wine districts in Australia noting
that, in the Riverina area, nearly all wineries used that system and some
continued to do so. Draining the potter fermenters was part of the normal

the potter tank. Once the juice was drained, the potter bin was moved below
the tank so that the skins could be removed from the tank. A small motor
"with gear reduction and drive chain" moved the potter bin and the bin
moved along a metal track that was set in the concrete floor. The motor was
engaged from a control box located at the end of the rails. To make the bins
move required the operator to hold down the button on the control box and
if the operator stopped holding down the button, the bin would stop. Mr
Vincent Bruno had used potter fermenters for many years as had other
members of his family and stated that he had never seen a potter bin move
when not powered. Prior to the accident involving Mr Gooley in March 2008,
he did not know that the bin could move when not powered.
9 In relation to the accident, Mr Vincent Bruno was of the view that the juice
had not drained properly due to a most unusual blockage above the base of

any pressure on the bottom door, it would have been very difficult to open

down on the door. After the accident the company de-commissioned the

any pressure on the bottom door, it would have been very difficult to open

10 The company was described as a small family business in an industry
that was competitive and volatile. Mr Vincent Bruno spoke of a number of
factors having an impact on consumption, including the strength of the
Australian dollar, reduced demand from overseas and an over supply of
wine both domestically and globally. There has been a decrease in wine
exports and an increase of wine made for the Australian domestic market. In
his view that made it extremely difficult to make a profit without
Government assistance. It was his view that, if Government assistance was
unavailable, the company would be making a substantial loss at the present
time.
11 Mr Vincent Bruno considered Mr Gooley to be a "good worker" who had
previously worked at the Winery. They were pleased to have him return for
the 2008 vintage to work as a Cellar Hand. He regretted the fatal injury

their relationship was more like that of friends. Many staff had been invited
and attended family weddings over many years and some of the staff had
contributed over 20 years' continuous service to the Winery while others
have reached 10 years' service. Following the accident, all staff were given
four days' paid leave and the Winery engaged a counsellor to assist staff
with group and individual counselling sessions. The Winery immediately
offered to pay for Mr Gooley's funeral and gave the funeral directors a
budget of $12,000. The company's workers compensation insurers
reimbursed the Winery for some of the costs of the funeral but that

offered to pay for Mr Gooley's funeral and gave the funeral directors a
budget of $12,000. The company's workers compensation insurers
reimbursed the Winery for some of the costs of the funeral but that
reimbursement was not requested or expected. Mr Vincent Bruno and his

In addition, Mr Gooley's partner was paid the wages that Mr Gooley would
have received for a period of six weeks following his death and this
amounted to over $4,000.
12 Mr Vincent Bruno had attended the Coronial Inquest in March and June
2009. At the Inquest he advised the Coroner that the Winery had replaced

On 10 February 2010, WorkCover issued a safety alert dealing with "mobile

were mentioned, including: ensuring that uncontrolled movement of the
bins was prevented by fitting brakes to the wheels or fitting mechanically

the potential crush points around the fermenter tanks were eliminated or
controlled; and, steps to prevent blockages.
13 Mr Robert Bruno had been employed at the Winery since 1997 and was
familiar with the Winery operated by his family. He was a qualified wine
maker having a tertiary qualification. He reported to the owners and
directors of the Winery, Mr Frank Bruno and Mr Vincent Bruno. He was
responsible for all aspects of production of the wine, including the bottling
line, warehousing and despatch. He has been the director of the Winery's
Safety Committee since 2007. The Committee had been formally meeting
since 2003.
14 Mr Robert Bruno was working at the Winery at the time of the accident
and gave assistance soon after Mr Gooley was injured. In his experience,
nothing like this incident had previously occurred at the Winery. The potter
fermenters had been in use in the Winery for approximately 25 years and he
had never seen the bin move in the way it had when Mr Gooley was injured.
He had only seen the bin move under power and he was unaware of any

fermenters had been in use in the Winery for approximately 25 years and he

He had only seen the bin move under power and he was unaware of any
early report of the bin moving when not powered. The potter bin system
was no longer used in the Winery and was replaced in its entirety after the
accident in 2008. In relation to Mr Gooley's history with the Winery, Mr
Robert Bruno spoke of him working during the 2005 vintage and also having

to be experienced and a good employee and in performing Cellar Hand
duties, he had been involved in operating plant such as the presses, filters
and potters as well as general cellar work. He spoke of continually thinking
about Mr Gooley.
15 Training had been provided for Mr Gooley and other casual staff by way
of a cellar induction course conducted by the Riverina Institute of Technical
and Further Education ("TAFE") A copy of the course outline attendance
summary was provided. That course was conducted over five days and
covered several aspects of health and safety, including working in confined

conducted by Mr Robert Bruno at the Winery before commencement of the

training, new employees were provided with a copy of the company's
general induction information and that was discussed with the employees.
The general induction information covered several pages and dealt with
some safety aspects in general terms. There was also a site induction
conducted by Mr Robert Bruno and involved taking new employees through
the Winery where an explanation was provided of the method of machinery
operation, potential hazards, and, the procedures to be adopted to avoid the
hazards. Employees were given a description of the general aspects of their
work and they were shown the location of personal protection equipment
and were told about the nature of the machinery used during vintage. Mr
Robert Bruno, during these discussions, drew attention to the pinch points
at the potter bin but not the potential pinch point that arose in the accident.
The company ruled that no one was allowed on the catwalk stage when the
potter bin was being moved. In the early stages of vintage the company
operated an informal buddy system where casual employees worked with
more experienced employees. Mr Gooley therefore would have received

The company ruled that no one was allowed on the catwalk stage when the
potter bin was being moved. In the early stages of vintage the company
operated an informal buddy system where casual employees worked with
more experienced employees. Mr Gooley therefore would have received
additional job guidance from his co-workers and supervisors.
16 Mr Robert Bruno explained the operation of the potters and the potter bin
in some detail. Much of that explanation also appears in the Agreed
Statement of Facts. Mr Gooley was engaged in the task of releasing skins
into the potter bin that was stationed below the tank. The potter bin was
moved below the tank so that it could capture the skins. The way the potter
bin was moved was by use of a small motor with "gear reduction and a drive
change" and that allowed the bin to move along l a metal track set in the
concrete floor. The motor was engaged by the operator continuously
depressing a button located on a control box situated at the end of the bin.
The motor would not engage unless the operator continuously pressed the
button so the bin would move. In that way the motor "acted as a brake" on
the potter bin. The location of the control box meant that the operator was

Robert Bruno's understanding of what happened in relation to the accident,
the draining of the potter fermenter stopped for an unknown reason and Mr
Gooley tried to open the door at the bottom of the tank. When the door seal
was released no more juice came out and under normal circumstances, any
remaining juice would leak out the side of the door and spray the operator
causing him to close the door. For an unknown reason this did not happen in
this incident and Mr Gooley proceeded to push the door aside. Normally,
when there was weight on the door from the skins it was impossible to slide
the door sideways. After the door opened all the way, the remaining weight
of the contents spilt out rapidly and caused the bin to move. Mr Robert
Bruno stated that he could not have imagined how this incident with Mr
Gooley could have occurred. He thought that he had the particular pinch
point hazard covered by not having a person on the catwalk stage when the
bin was being moved and he had not thought that the bin would move when
not powered. He had also never considered that juice could be stuck in the
potter tank without being detected because of the opening mechanism of
the door.

bin was being moved and he had not thought that the bin would move when
not powered. He had also never considered that juice could be stuck in the

17 During the 2008 vintage a standard operating procedure was in use at
the Winery. Mr Robert Bruno had developed the procedure from his
experience of working in the Winery and was assisted by other people who
had also worked there. In writing the standard procedure, the job was
analysed in depth with experienced operators and by this process, control

identified to enable the job to be performed in a safe and efficient manner
while maintaining the quality of the product. This was not specified as a risk
assessment but he believed that the process was a similar process to
performing a risk assessment and should be considered as contributing to
the risk assessment process. Part of the standard operating procedure
related to the draining of the potter fermenters. That standard operating
procedure identified hazards and stated that, when moving the potter bin,
all care was to be taken to make sure that nobody was standing on the bin
platform while the bin was moving. The documents stated that there were
major pinch points on the platform and only the operator was to move the
potter bin. Power to the bin was to be turned off when it was not in use.
18 After the accident involving Mr Gooley on 13 March 2008, the potter bin
was chained when draining took place of the three remaining potter
fermenters and this was done to prevent any inadvertent movement. After
that drainage was completed, in-depth consideration was given to the way
in which the process could be changed and the defendant company
concluded that the whole potter fermentation system should be replaced.
The defendant company did not consider that other systems recommended
by WorkCover were adequate as there was no elimination of the pinch point
and an employee could forget to chock the wheels on the potter bin. These
suggestions were additions to the existing system rather than requiring
replacement of the system.
19 The defendant company also engaged an occupational health and safety
consultant who assisted in documenting procedures and safety systems for
the company. The consultant prepared a comprehensive report. The
company had taken additional safety initiatives such as participating in
WorkCover's mentoring programme. When the company originally applied
to participate in the programme there was no mentor available but on the
second occasion the defendant company was paired with a much larger

company had taken additional safety initiatives such as participating in
WorkCover's mentoring programme. When the company originally applied
to participate in the programme there was no mentor available but on the
second occasion the defendant company was paired with a much larger
winery in the region. The programme spanned an eight-month period and
involved one-on-one discussions, information sessions, workshop and site
visits. Through this mentoring programme Mr Robert Bruno had the
opportunity to utilise the resources and experience of the large winery in
relation to health and safety and learned a great deal from the programme.
He implemented ideas from the programme into the operations of the
Winery. In March 2008 he was a "driving force" behind the regional
Occupational Health and Safety Committee made up of other wineries in the
Riverina region. That Committee now meets bi-monthly and discusses
health and safety issues in wineries. The Committee had made significant
progress in developing training courses for winery workers and improving
communication between wineries on safety and hazard arrangements. As a
result of the activities of the Committee the wine industry in the Riverina
had experienced significant reduction in workplace injuries, particularly
chemical related injuries. In approximately August and September 2008
WorkCover conducted advisory visits to wineries in New South Wales and on
these visits, no improvement notices were issued to the defendant
company.
20 Mr Robert Bruno was the current director of the defendant company's
Safety Committee and had been so since 2007. The Committee had met
formally since 2003 and employees were encouraged to report any health
and safety issues to the Committee. The Committee met bi-monthly or as
necessary to discuss issues raised by employees, managers or committee
members. Since 2003, the Committee, through its associated work, had
made significant progress in transforming the Winery from a small, older
style winery into a modern facility. Minutes of the Committee meetings were
available and displayed for employees to review. It was noted that, upon
consideration of these documents, they showed that no one had identified
the problem that had arisen when Mr Gooley was fatally injured. The
defendant also issued newsletters to employees that included relevant
health and safety issues and more recently it had begun to conduct formal
weekly toolbox meetings where health and safety issues were discussed as
required.
21 Training for new employees was provided by the defendant company in a
number of ways. Firstly, there was a requirement to attend the cellar
induction course conducted by the Riverina TAFE and secondly, the
company conducted its site induction involving an explanation of the

21 Training for new employees was provided by the defendant company in a
number of ways. Firstly, there was a requirement to attend the cellar
induction course conducted by the Riverina TAFE and secondly, the
company conducted its site induction involving an explanation of the
Winery's relevant standard operating procedure and a walk-through of the
plant where hazards were identified and procedures explained. Lastly, the
Winery used the informal buddy system at the beginning of each vintage
where more experienced employees were paired with casuals to assist them
with on-the-job learning.
22 In relation to support provided to Mr Gooley's family, Mr Robert Bruno
said that he visited Mr Gooley's partner two days after the accident and
expressed his sadness for her loss. He had also attended Mr Gooley's
funeral and described it as a difficult time. It remained a difficult memory
and he still regularly thought about the accident. The defendant company
met the costs of Mr Gooley's funeral and provided financial assistance to Mr
Gooley's partner.
DELIBERATION
23 The Court accepts that its primary task is establishing the objective
seriousness of the offence. The prosecutor has drawn attention to the
particulars in the Amended Application for Order in relation to which the
defendant has entered its plea of guilty. Those particulars were submitted to
constitute a "broad or multi-faceted breach touching on a number of
different aspects of the defendant's operation". The acts and omissions of
the defendant included unsafe plant in that the potter bin could be
inadvertently moved and that the interaction between the potter bin
platform and the vinomatic platform created a pinch point and otherwise did
not comply with Australian Standards as well as a lack of a safe system of
work, a failure to undertake an adequate risk assessment and a failure to
provide adequate information, instruction and training to the company's
employees. That broad or multi-faceted breach, nevertheless, focused on
the operation of the potter bin.
24 The written submissions for the prosecutor identified the range of acts or
omissions by the defendant that demonstrated the seriousness of the
offence. It is convenient to reproduce the substance of that submission:
15. The particular alleging unsafe plant focuses first on the
inadvertent movement of the potter bin (including the potter bin
platform) when it was not powered. Prior to the incident on 13
March 2008 the defendant had not experienced the unexpected
or inadvertent movement of the potter bin when the motor was

platform) when it was not powered. Prior to the incident on 13
March 2008 the defendant had not experienced the unexpected
or inadvertent movement of the potter bin when the motor was
not engaged. However, it was revealed during the investigation
that the potter bin could be moved with considerable force when
it was not powered ... The defendant failed to implement a
system of moveable wheel chocks or wheel brakes to be installed
on the metal tracks on which the potter bin moves ...
16. The defendant has admitted that it provided unsafe plant
because of the creation of a pinch point by the interaction of the
potter bin platform and the vinomatic platform. The two
platforms operated to allow the potter bin platform to travel
underneath the adjacent vinomatic platform, hence they
interacted to create a pinch point between the edge of the potter
bin and the edge of the vinomatic platform ...
17. The interaction between the two platforms resulted in a
clearance between the edge of the potter bin and the edge of the
vinomatic platform of only 120mm. The relevant Australian
Standard provided that the minimum gap to avoid crushing to
the head is 300mm and the minimum gap to avoid crushing
injuries to the body is 500mm ...
18. The distance from the floor of the potter bin platform to the
floor of the adjacent vinomatic platform was only 1.4 metres. The
relevant Australian Standard provides that the vertical clearance
above platforms and walkways shall not be less than 2000mm ...
19. The defendant had identified the hazard of the pinch points.
It was referred to in the Standard Operating Procedures ("SOP")
for the process of pressing potters in a general fashion, that is
"There are major pinch points on the platform". ... The SOP did
not identify the locations of particular pinch points. Robert Bruno
stated that, as part of the induction for new employees who were
working in the cellar area, he would show the employees the
pinch points. This was not documented. Two employees - Mr
Becher and Mr Torbuck did not recall being shown the major
pinch points ...
20. In addition to attending induction at the premises, Mr Gooley
attended a cellar induction course at the Riverina Institute. Mr
Gooley would have received some on the job training at the
workplace. However, the defendant was unaware whether any
specific training had been provided to Mr Gooley in relation to
the task of pressing the potters ...

Gooley would have received some on the job training at the
workplace. However, the defendant was unaware whether any
specific training had been provided to Mr Gooley in relation to
the task of pressing the potters ...
21. The defendant failed to provide and maintain a safe system
of work in that it failed to ensure that pinch points were
identified to employees. The defendant failed to conduct an
adequate risk assessment of the task of pressing the potters in
that it failed to identify adequately the risk of injury arising from
the pinch points and the risk could be controlled.
22. The defendant failed to provide adequate information
instruction and training about the use and operation of the potter
bin (including the platform) and the vinomatic platform.
25 It was then submitted for the prosecutor that the risk particularised was
the risk of employees being exposed to risk of injury from being hit, trapped
or crushed by moving plant. That risk was reasonably foreseeable and was
foreseen by the defendant. The risk had been identified by the defendant in
a general fashion having regard to the terms of the Standard Operating
Procedure. The risk was also said to be evident from a visual inspection of
the two platforms and the way in which they interacted to create the pinch
point. The defendant had tried to control the risk by relying on the Standard
Operating Procedure as an instruction that nobody was to be on the potter
bin platform while the bin was being moved. The defendant, however, did
not turn its mind to the circumstances in which the potter bin could move
and assumed that it would only move when powered. If a proper risk
assessment had been conducted, it would have disclosed the
abovementioned risks. The defendant had not undertaken an adequate risk
assessment to determine when the risk could arise. It was further submitted
that it would be a serious offence where there was an obvious or
foreseeable risk to safety against which appropriate steps were not taken,
even though such measures were available and feasible. The prosecutor
then submitted that the inadvertent movement of the potter bin could have
been controlled by the use of wheel chocks or wheel brakes. There could
have been a system of clearly identifying and reinforcing with the
employees the risk of pinch points. These measures could have been
introduced to eliminate or reduce the risks prior to the accident. The
objective seriousness of the breach was therefore compounded because
these measures were not taken.
26 While the submissions for the defendant appeared to accept the serious

introduced to eliminate or reduce the risks prior to the accident. The
objective seriousness of the breach was therefore compounded because
these measures were not taken.
26 While the submissions for the defendant appeared to accept the serious
nature of the defendant's breach, especially by categorising it as an offence
that would appropriately fall in the middle range of offences, the defendant
challenged the degree of foreseeability and the appropriateness of some of
the suggested simple steps that could be taken to address the risk. It was
submitted that the risk was not clearly foreseeable and arose in the context
of an "inadvertent movement" of the potter bin when it was not powered
and a pinch point that was created by such inadvertent movement. It was
submitted that the potter system was not limited to the defendant and had
been used throughout Australia and the wine industry for 30 years. The
occurrence of this accident had prompted WorkCover to issue an alert
concerning the use of potter overhead fermentation tanks and mobile bins.
In the 30 years since the equipment had been installed, the defendant had
not experienced unexpected or inadvertent movement of the potter bin
when the motor was disengaged. It was not until the investigation of the
accident that it was revealed that the potter bin could be moved with
considerable force along the metal track when the bin was not powered. The
defendant's position was, up until this accident, it was unaware that the
potter bin could move when not powered and that the motor acted as a
brake on the bin. In those circumstances, the nature of the risk was not
"clearly foreseeable" as submitted by the prosecutor. Ultimately, the
defendant did not accept that using moveable wheel chocks or wheel brakes
as suggested by WorkCover was an adequate measure and so removed the
moveable bins and replaced the entire potter fermentation system.
27 It was also contested that a risk assessment would have shown the risk
of the bin moving and it was further submitted that there was no evidence
to support a finding that the chock would be effective to stop the bin from
moving. These matters had to be considered in the further context of a long
running business that had addressed safety in its workplace and where
there had been no prior breach and no experience of the circumstances that
occurred on the day of Mr Gooley's accident.
28 There are cases where the injuries received provide evidence that is

running business that had addressed safety in its workplace and where
there had been no prior breach and no experience of the circumstances that
occurred on the day of Mr Gooley's accident.
28 There are cases where the injuries received provide evidence that is
indicative of the seriousness of the risk - this is such a case. The method of
operation adopted at the Winery involved large and heavy pieces of
equipment that were moveable with those pieces of equipment operating
close to a fixed walkway. While the seriousness of the breach cannot be
doubted, there is substance in the defendant's point about the degree of
foreseeability of the risk. The defendant's submissions on this aspect were
restrained and inferentially accepted a degree of foreseeability and so
adopted the description that the risk was not "clearly foreseeable". It can be
accepted that, over such a long period of time of operating this equipment
without any hint that the potter bin would move, it might give rise to an
expectation that the motor was in fact holding the moveable bin. Having
had the assistance of a description of the method of operation, especially by
reference to numerous photographs, it is entirely likely that no more than
the weight of this very large moveable bin was the primary reason that it
had not been found to move over these many years of operation. It was only
in most unusual circumstances where substantial force was applied that it
was found that the bin would move. In that respect it appears that the
combination of the unusual clogging of the overheard bins leading to the
unexpected rush of product provided such a degree of force that the potter
bin actually moved and crushed Mr Gooley. In that context it can be
accepted that the risk was not "clearly foreseeable" although there were
aspects of this system where there was a clearer foreseeability. A properly
conducted risk assessment that paid attention to the relevant standards
dealing with the safety of machinery and the safe distances and safety gaps
required would then have to consider the possibility that the moveable bin
might move when the motor was not engaged. The existence of a risk is not
established simply by an experience of an event where a particular risk
arose but may also be assessed by having regard to the possibilities where
otherwise there is no experience of a specific event. Nevertheless, in this
regard, there is some force in the defendant's submissions in relation to
these matters.
29 In relation to the suggested efficacy of a chock against the wheel of the

otherwise there is no experience of a specific event. Nevertheless, in this
regard, there is some force in the defendant's submissions in relation to
these matters.
29 In relation to the suggested efficacy of a chock against the wheel of the
potter bin to prevent it moving, the demonstration of the bin under power
being held by a chock, regardless of the weight of the contents of the bins,
does suggest that chocks and certainly, if not chocks, then brakes would
have been simple and effective measures to prevent the bin from moving. It
also appears that the interim measure adopted by the defendant, namely,
chaining the bin in place, was also simple and effective in preventing the
risk of movement from arising. As to the complaint that not all of the
induction was documented, the utility of a documented system has to be
weighed against the nature of the task and the employment. To the extent
that casual employees were used during vintage, it might be expecting too
much of them to study and memorise written directives and there are
undoubtedly circumstances in which clear, on-the-job instruction will be
effective. These matters have all been taken into account in concluding that
this was, nevertheless, a serious breach.
30 It was submitted for the defendant that general and specific deterrence
were not significant elements in determining an appropriate penalty in this
case. That submission was put forward on the basis that this was an unusual
accident arising from an admittedly inadvertent movement of a bin in
circumstances where there had been no previous experience over a long
period of time of such an occurrence. In relation to specific deterrence, it
was submitted that, although the defendant continued to operate in the
industry, it could not be said that the defendant did not have a commitment
to safety prior to the accident. The steps taken since the accident
demonstrated the intensified efforts of the defendant in matters of safety.
Those matters may be readily accepted but both general and specific
deterrence are matters of significance in this case although tempered by
the above considerations. The circumstances surrounding this accident,
however, indicate the level of ongoing diligence required of employers in
relation to the workplace and how they should not be lulled into a false
sense of the adequacy of their safety systems simply because there has not
been any previous adverse or dangerous event. Detailed risk assessments
are a valuable part of such diligence in safety in the operation of heavy
equipment in the workplace. The safety record of the defendant and the

been any previous adverse or dangerous event. Detailed risk assessments
are a valuable part of such diligence in safety in the operation of heavy
equipment in the workplace. The safety record of the defendant and the
important steps taken to address this risk in its operations does lead to
specific deterrence playing a lesser role.
31 In relation to subjective factors, the prosecutor accepted, as does the
Court, that properly viewed this is an early plea. There is no reason why, in
those circumstances, that the defendant should not receive a discount of 25
per cent for the utilitarian value of that plea. Similarly, the prosecutor has
accepted, as does the Court, that there is evidence of their remorse and
contrition and that the defendant has publicly accepted responsibility for
the accident and has not only committed substantial financial amounts to
rectify omissions in their system but on a personal basis, gave financial
support to Mr Gooley's family. It is accepted that the defendant is a good
corporate citizen without prior offences and thus is entitled to the leniency
attendant upon that status. It has a long history of operation where safety
was considered and addressed in the ways referred to in the evidence. It
has taken considerable remedial steps to address the risk demonstrated by
this tragic event and has addressed its own safety systems on a wider basis
with the assistance of a consultant. The defendant has also engaged in
wide-ranging activities in relation to promoting safety in the workplace in
this industry and appears to have taken a leadership role in the Riverina
area. Importantly, the defendant co-operated with the WorkCover
investigation. Although some evidence was given concerning the state of
the wine market and the profitability of the defendant, that material
provided background information only and no application was made
pursuant to the provisions of the Fines Act 1996. All of those matters will be
taken into account in mitigating the ultimate penalty to be imposed.
32 It is appropriate at this point to note that, in the course of proceedings,
the prosecutor tendered Victim Impact Statements from Ms Renee
Bloomfield, Mr Gooley's partner, and two children of the family, Emika
Gooley and Toby Vant. Ms Bloomfield read her statement to the Court and
described in detail how the loss of her partner had affected her life and the
adverse consequences suffered by her children. The Court extended its
condolences to the family for their loss. Having determined that a conviction
will be entered against the defendant, those statements are received and

adverse consequences suffered by her children. The Court extended its
condolences to the family for their loss. Having determined that a conviction
will be entered against the defendant, those statements are received and
will be considered by the Court.
ORDERS
33 Having regard to the abovementioned matters, the Court makes the
following orders:
(a) the defendant, Toorak Winery Pty Ltd, is found guilty of a breach of s
8(1) of the Occupational Health and Safety Act 2000 as particularised in
the Amended Application for Order in Matter No IRC 183 of 2010 to
which it entered a plea of guilty;
(b) the defendant is fined the sum of $125,000 with half that sum to be
paid to the prosecutor by way of moiety;
(c) the defendant is to pay the costs of the prosecutor in a sum as
agreed or, in the absence of agreement, as assessed or otherwise
ordered by the Court.
ANNEXURE
AGREED STATEMENT OF FACTS
1. At all material times the Prosecutor, Inspector Simone Yates, was duly
appointed under Division 1 of Part 5 of the Occupational Health and
Safety Act 2000 (“the Act”) and empowered under Section 106 of the
said Act to institute proceedings in this matter.
2. TOORAK WINERY PTY LTD (“the defendant”) is and was at all
material times, a corporation,
Background
3. At all material times the defendant was an employer conducting a
business involving the production, packaging and sale of wines.
4. Mr Francesco (Frank) Bruno Jnr and Mr Vincent Bruno were directors
of the defendant. In their capacities as directors, Vincent Bruno was
responsible for sales and administration and Frank Bruno was
responsible for overseeing the operation of the vineyard.
5. As at 13 March 2008 the defendant employed six full time staff and
approximately four casuals. During the vintage period extra casual staff
were employed for approximately six weeks.
The vintage period is from mid February to early April each year. During
this time staff are required to work twelve-hour shifts and twelve days a
fortnight. Employees generally worked twelve-hour shifts Monday to
Friday and either a full or half shift on a Saturday, depending on
workload demand.
6. Raymond Gooley commenced employment with the defendant as a
casual cellarhand on 15 October 2007. Mr Gooley had prior experience
as a cellarhand and had previously worked for the defendant during the
2004 vintage. His duties involved operating plant (including the press,

casual cellarhand on 15 October 2007. Mr Gooley had prior experience
as a cellarhand and had previously worked for the defendant during the
2004 vintage. His duties involved operating plant (including the press,
potter bin and potters) and general cellar work. Mr Gooley had
completed at the instigation of the Defendant, a Cellar Induction course
through the Riverina Institute - Technical and Advanced Education,
Griffith Campus.
The Potter Bin and the Potters
7. At all material times, the defendant owned and operated a large steel
hopper (“the potter bin”), and six steel fermentation tanks. The potter
bin and fermentation tanks were manufactured by A & G Engineering
and were approximately 30 years old and had not been modified since
installation. The particular potter bin system manufactured by A & G
Engineering is commonly used within the wine industry.
8. The fermentation tanks, which are commonly known as “potters”, are
situated on a frame above the potter bin and are labelled P1 to P6. The
potters are suspended approximately 3 metres above ground so that
gravity can be used to empty them. The potters are filled with juice and
skins and allowed to ferment for approximately 5 days before being
pressed and the skins and juice separated. Each potter holds
approximately 6 000 litres of juice (“must”).
9. The potter bin is used to transfer the crushed grapes and must from
the potters to the press. The potter bin is not large enough to sit under
all six potters so it has to be moved under the particular potter that is
being emptied.
10. The potter bin measures 4.6 metres wide, 3.8 metres deep and 1.85
metres in height. The inside walls of the potter bin are at an angle of
approximately 45 degrees and two augers are located at the bottom of
the potter bin.
11. The potter bin is mounted upon a large steel frame. The frame sits
on four metal wheels and runs on a metal track, which is set into the
concrete floor. At each end of the tracks are small triangular shaped
metal stoppers. The distance between the front and end stoppers is 8
metres.
12. The potter bin is moved by a small motor with gear reduction and
drive chain. Control boxes located on the eastern and western side of
the potter bin frame control the movement of the potter bin along the
tracks. To engage the motor the operator must continuously depress a

drive chain. Control boxes located on the eastern and western side of
the potter bin frame control the movement of the potter bin along the
tracks. To engage the motor the operator must continuously depress a
button on the switch. If the button is not continuously depressed the
motor will not engage.
13. At the rear of the potter bin is a small deck (“the potter bin platform
or lower deck”) which is welded to the support frame. The deck is 700
metres wide and 1.5 metres above ground level. Adjacent to the potter
bin platform is a stationery catwalk known as the upper deck, or
vinomatic work platform. This platform allows access to a vinomatic
machine and to the top of the potter tanks. The distance from the floor
of the potter bin platform (lower deck) to the floor of the adjacent
vinomatic work platform (upper deck) is 1.4 metres.
The Work Being Performed at the Time of the Incident
14. At the time of the incident Mr Gooley was undertaking a process
known as “pressing potters”. This process involved draining the juice
from the potter tank via a press and transferring the juice into a wine
storage tank.
15. As part of this process the juice would initially be drained from the
potter via a draining hose. When the flow of juice stopped the hose
would be drained out manually and the potter bin rolled below the tank
to be emptied.
16. A small six inch valve located at the base of the potter would then be
opened to release any remaining juice left in the potter. After the juice
had stopped draining from the value, a large door on the potter would
be opened so that the skins could drop into the potter bin. If there were
still skins in the potter then a pitchfork was used to manually dig the
skins out.
17. The skins were then augured out of the potter bin into a press so
that the remainder of the juice was separated from the skins.
18. The procedure for pressing potters would generally take three to
four hours per potter.
The Events of 13 March 2008
19. At 6.00am on 13 March 2008 Mr Gooley commenced his 12 hour day
shift at the premises. At the changeover of shifts Mr Gooley was
assigned the task of pressing potter P4 during his shift.
20. Mr Tornbuck (cellar hand) was operating the crusher and Mr Lawson,
(shift supervisor) was unloading grape bins from the truck into the
crusher.

assigned the task of pressing potter P4 during his shift.
20. Mr Tornbuck (cellar hand) was operating the crusher and Mr Lawson,
(shift supervisor) was unloading grape bins from the truck into the
crusher.
21. At approximately 11.30am Mr Gooley went to the crusher and asked
Mr Lawson to assist him to open a 150mm butterfly valve at the base of
P4. This valve was a release valve that drains the juice remaining in the
potter into the potter bin. Mr Gooley stood on the potter bin platform
attached to the potter bin and Mr Lawson stood on the ground beside
the potter bin. Together they opened the valve; however not much juice
drained out of the valve. Mr Lawson stated that they assumed that most
of the juice had already drained out.
22. Mr Lawson returned to the crusher area and left Mr Gooley to finish
emptying the contents of the potter into the potter bin. Mr Gooley then
had the task of undoing the main bottom door of the potter, so that the
skins could drop into the potter bin. Mr Lawson stated that Mr Gooley
remained on the potter bin platform whilst performing this task.
23. Immediately after Mr Lawson left Mr Gooley, Mr Doering, a truck
driver, noticed a spray of juice on the ground and alerted Mr Lawson. Mr
Lawson assumed that there was a split must line and instructed Mr
Torbuck to stop the crusher. Mr Lawson went to investigate the source of
the must and found that it was, in fact, ferment. He then realised that it
must have come from the area where Mr Gooley was working.
24. Mr Lawson and Mr Torbuck ran to where Mr Gooley was working and
observed that he was pinned between the potter bin and the adjacent
vinomatic platform.
25. Mr Lawson, Mr Torbuck and Mr Doering attempted to manually move
the potter bin but were unable to do so due to the weight of the bin. Mr
Peter Draper, (maintenance worker) was subsequently instructed to
unscrew the stationary platform so as to free Mr Gooley.
26. An ambulance attended the scene shortly after the incident,
however Mr Gooley was declared dead on arrival.
27. Following the incident, it was found that there was approximately
2000 litres of wine in storage tank D41 from potter P4. If the full amount
of wine had drained out into the storage tank, then the expected
amount should have been around 6000 litres.

2000 litres of wine in storage tank D41 from potter P4. If the full amount
of wine had drained out into the storage tank, then the expected
amount should have been around 6000 litres.
28. It appears that the incident occurred when Mr Gooley opened the
bottom door of the potter and the remaining contents came out rapidly,
hitting the sides of the potter bin. The substantial force of the expelled
contents then caused the potter bin to move, trapping Mr Gooley
between the edge of the potter bin and the stationary platform.
Investigation of the Incident
29. On 13 March 2008, Inspector Simone Yates and Inspector Stuart
Larkin attended the premises of the defendant and made observations
contained in a Factual Inspection Report dated 13 March 2008.
30. On 18 March 2008, Inspector Yates attended the premises for a
follow up inspection and made observations contained in a Factual
Inspection Report dated 18 March 2008
31. During the course of the inspections at the premises a number of
photographs were taken.
Unsafe Plant
32. The defendant failed to ensure that the potter bin could not move
inadvertently when not powered. The potter bin operated on a track and
the motor to move the potter bin would not engage unless it was turned
on and a button was continually depressed by the operator. The
defendant failed to implement a system of moveable wheel chocks, or
wheel brakes, to be installed on the metal tracks on which the potter bin
moves, which would prevent the inadvertent movement of the potter
bin.
33. There were metal stoppers located at the end of the tracks upon
which the potter bin operated. However the metal stoppers were located
in such a position that allowed for the potter bin platform to travel
underneath the adjacent vinomatic platform. Accordingly the platforms
would interact in such a way that they created a pinch point between
the edge of the potter bin and the edge of the vinomatic platform. The
clearance between the edge of the potter bin and the edge of the
vinomatic platform was only 120mm. In this regard, Australian Standard
AS 4024.1 – 2006, Safety of Machinery, Part 1803: Safety distances and
safety gaps, Section 5.2 – “minimum gaps to prevent crushing of parts
of the human body”, provides that the minimum gap to avoid crushing
to the head is 300mm and the minimum gap to avoid crushing injuries
to the body is 500mm.
34. Further the distance from the floor of the potter bin platform (lower

of the human body”, provides that the minimum gap to avoid crushing
to the head is 300mm and the minimum gap to avoid crushing injuries
to the body is 500mm.
34. Further the distance from the floor of the potter bin platform (lower
deck) to the floor of the adjacent vinomatic platform (upper deck) was
only 1.4 metres. Australian Standard AS 1657-1992 Fixed platforms,
walkways, stairways and ladders – Design, construction and installation,
states at Section 3.1.4, “Minimum Vertical Clearance”:
Except where otherwise approved by the regulatory authority,
the vertical clearance above platforms and walkways shall be not
less than 2000 mm.
35. The defendant had not previously experienced unexpected or
inadvertent movement of the bin when the motor was not engaged.
However the investigation revealed that the potter bin could be moved,
with considerable force, along the metal tracks when the potter bin was
not powered. As such, the defendant did not ensure that the movement
of the potter bin was controlled or restricted so as to prevent the potter
bin from inadvertent or unexpected movement when the motor was not
engaged.
Systems of Work Prior to the Incident
36. At the time of the incident the defendant had not carried out a
formal documented risk assessment with respect to the operation and
use of the potters or potter bin.
37. Further no formal risk assessment had been conducted in relation to
the task of pressing potters. According to Mr Robert Bruno informal risk
assessments were however undertaken by anyone who was working on
the potters.
38. The defendant had a Standard Operating Procedure (“SOP”) in place
for the process of pressing potters. A written copy of the SOP was
provided to each employee who worked in the cellar area.
39. The SOP identified the following hazard in relation to pressing
potters:
Hazards
When moving the potter bin all care must be taken to make sure
there is nobody standing on the bin platform while the bin is
being moved. There are major pinch points on the platform. Only
the operator must move the potter bin and the bin must be
turned off when not in use.
40. The SOP did not however identify the locations of the particular
pinch points.
41. Mr Robert Bruno understood the major pinch points identified in the
SOP to be where the bin meets the adjacent catwalk of the vinomatic.
He stated that the pinch points were shown to employees as part of

pinch points.
41. Mr Robert Bruno understood the major pinch points identified in the
SOP to be where the bin meets the adjacent catwalk of the vinomatic.
He stated that the pinch points were shown to employees as part of
their induction training at the commencement of the season.
42. However both Mr Becher and Mr Torbuck did not recall recall being
shown the major pinch points. Mr Becher was aware of the pinch points
through his own experience and observations at the premises; but Mr
Torbruck was not familiar with the pinch points, although he did state he
knew of a danger.
Training, Information and Instruction
43. The defendant provided new employees with a site safety induction
upon commencement at the premises. Some, but not all, of the
defendant’s site safety induction was documented.
44. The defendant did not have a formal system of training in place at
the premises, however on-the-job training was provided by various
employees at the premises. At the time of the incident there was no
register or training records documenting any of the training provided to
employees.
45. The defendant did not provide adequate information or instruction to
its employees with respect to the safe use and operation of the potter
bin and the vinomatic platform. The defendant did not provide sufficient
information regarding the hazards associated with the use of the plant,
and in particular with respect to the dangers associated with moveable
bins. Further the defendant did not provide adequate information and
instruction regarding the location of all the pinch points on the potter bin
platform, nor did the defendant ensure that employees were informed
that the potter bin platform could move underneath the vinomatic
platform and cause a possible crush injury.
46. The defendant did not provide adequate training with respect to the
task of pressing potters; nor did not undertake any assessment as to
whether its employees were competent to carry out the task of pressing
potters.
47. The defendant was unaware whether any specific training had been
provided to Mr Gooley in relation to the task of pressing potters. Mr
Lawson (shift supervisor) and Mr Becher (leading hand/supervisor) were
also unaware of any specific training that Mr Gooley had received with
respect to pressing grapes or how often he had carried out the task
previously. Mr Lawson assumed that Mr Gooley had been pressing
potters during the time he worked on the night shift. However Mr Becher
stated that Mr Gooley had not pressed any grapes during the time he

previously. Mr Lawson assumed that Mr Gooley had been pressing
potters during the time he worked on the night shift. However Mr Becher
stated that Mr Gooley had not pressed any grapes during the time he
worked on night shift. Mr Becher assumed that, based on his confidence,
Mr Gooley had undertaken the task before.
Systems of work following the incident
48. On 13 March 2008, the defendant was issued with a Prohibition
Notice (No. 147855), directing that the potter fermenter must not be
used as part of the production process until the contaminated product
was disposed of and a clearance was obtained by a competent person.
The defendant engaged an Environmental Health & Building Surveyor
from the Leeton Shire Council to provide advice regarding the
compliance requirements.
49. On 18 March 2009 the defendant was issued with a further
Prohibition Notice (No. 147856), preventing the potter bin from being
used until a safe system of work was developed to ensure that the
movement of the potter bin was controlled and restricted.
50. The defendant subsequently removed and decommissioned the
potter bin involved in the subject incident. The potters are now used as
liquid storage tanks only. An alternative method is in place to ferment
and press red grapes.
51. Since the incident the defendant has also appointed the services of
an occupational health and safety consultant, Mr Ian Burn from “Safety
Doctor” and has carried out a risk assessment on the task of pressing
potters.
52. Since the incident the Defendant has participated in WorkCover’s
mentor program. Additionally the Defendant has initiated a regional
occupational health and safety committee comprising of several wineries
in the region and is an active member of that committee. The Defendant
has also sought feedback from WorkCover inspectors about its activities
and initiatives that it has implemented in respect of occupational health
and safety.
Co-operation with WorkCover
53. The defendant co-operated with WorkCover during the investigation.
The Defendant 's Criminal History
54. The defendant has no prior criminal convictions in NSW.
